query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr has 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but its poor oxygen resistance limits practical high-temperature use. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing the alloy’s useful mechanical performance? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention and mechanism, the predicted change relative to untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr, the relevant temperature, atmosphere, exposure time, and mechanical-loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: 3D ink extrusion printing followed by de-binding in flowing hydrogen, and vacuum sintering at 1400°C for 18 hours with titanium sponge oxygen getter applied to Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr ink blend containing hydride powders (HfH2, NbH, TaH0.5, TiH2, ZrH2) and metallic Ti/Nb, dispersed in a polystyrene/binder matrix will act through Sequential decomposition of hydrides driven by formation enthalpy differences (Ta→Nb→Hf/Ti/Zr), enabling in-situ alloying and oxygen scavenging and Interstitial strengthening from controlled oxygen uptake (≈1.0 wt.%) combined with phase stabilization; quenching suppresses alpha-HCP formation to retain metastable beta-BCC; silicide coating provides oxidation resistance via self-healing (Zr,Hf)O2 oxide filling, giving Nearly fully dense bulk with metastable single beta-BCC phase (after quench) and excellent high-temperature compression strength; significant reduction in oxidation rate compared to uncoated baseline relative to Cast HfNbTaTiZr or uncoated sintered samples prone to cracking, alpha-HCP embrittlement, and rapid oxidation (k ≈ 570 mg² cm⁻⁴ h⁻¹).
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr ink blend containing hydride powders (HfH2, NbH, TaH0.5, TiH2, ZrH2) and metallic Ti/Nb, dispersed in a polystyrene/binder matrix
generation.intervention: 3D ink extrusion printing followed by de-binding in flowing hydrogen, and vacuum sintering at 1400°C for 18 hours with titanium sponge oxygen getter
generation.conditions: Vacuum atmosphere (<3×10⁻⁶ torr), sequential heating to 1400°C, followed by water quenching from 1500°C for phase stabilization
generation.structural_mediator: Sequential decomposition of hydrides driven by formation enthalpy differences (Ta→Nb→Hf/Ti/Zr), enabling in-situ alloying and oxygen scavenging
generation.mechanism: Interstitial strengthening from controlled oxygen uptake (≈1.0 wt.%) combined with phase stabilization; quenching suppresses alpha-HCP formation to retain metastable beta-BCC; silicide coating provides oxidation resistance via self-healing (Zr,Hf)O2 oxide filling
generation.predicted_outcome: Nearly fully dense bulk with metastable single beta-BCC phase (after quench) and excellent high-temperature compression strength; significant reduction in oxidation rate compared to uncoated baseline
generation.baseline: Cast HfNbTaTiZr or uncoated sintered samples prone to cracking, alpha-HCP embrittlement, and rapid oxidation (k ≈ 570 mg² cm⁻⁴ h⁻¹)
generation.boundary: Oxygen content must be maintained around 1.0 wt.%; cooling rate dictates phase stability (slow cooling yields alpha+beta, quenching yields single beta); sintering time must exceed 15 min to achieve full densification

falsification_experiment.design: In-situ X-ray diffraction monitoring of hydride decomposition onset temperatures and phase shifts during heating; post-quench XRD/EBSD for phase identification and grain size (target ~33 µm)
measurements: In-situ X-ray diffraction monitoring of hydride decomposition onset temperatures and phase shifts during heating; post-quench XRD/EBSD for phase identification and grain size (target ~33 µm)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the predicted outcome is not observed relative to the baseline, the hypothesis is rejected.
